title: Communication patterns — KV-cache coalescing & packetization exploration
content:
Purpose: Explore how communication packetization and host-side coalescing of KV-cache requests affect tail latency and throughput for multi-GPU inference. We want to know: when does coalescing help vs hurt, how NCCL packetization interacts with small-token workloads, and what knobs (driver/abi/NCCL) give us the best SLOs for short prompt inference on 8+ GPU nodes.

Background/context:
- Observed higher-than-expected p50->p99 jump on short-inference workloads (seq_len=8-32) after a rollout that changed our KV cache placement. Suspect interaction of small-message patterns with NCCL and NIC packetization.
- Related tickets: JIRA-RT-842 (user-visible tail spike on small prompts), previous notes on small-packet interleaving tail latency.

Hypotheses to validate:
1) Small, frequent KV fetches generate microbursts that suffer from host/NIC batching limits — resulting in tail-latency amplification when messages aren't coalesced.
2) Aggressive coalescing (on host) can reduce driver/NIC overhead but increases per-request headroom (waiting for coalesce window) and therefore increases p50 for tiny requests; the tradeoff point depends on request arrival distribution.
3) NCCL segmentation / packetization parameters can change the effective wire-level fragmentation; certain values amplify serialization at the rail (NVLink/PCIe) leading to poorer throughput under fine-grained access.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Workloads: synthetic token-gen microbench (Poisson arrivals), replay of production request traces (sample of short prompt traffic), and a stress-run of batched long sequences to check throughput regression.
- Topologies: single-node (8x A100 80GB), multi-node (2x 8x A100), mixed NVLink island (4 + 4 with no NVLink between islands).
- Variables: host coalescing window (0, 50us, 250us, 1ms), max_coalesce_bytes (1KB, 8KB, 64KB), NCCL_PROTO (simple/intra/plls), NCCL_P2P_LEVEL (SYS, SHM), GDRCOPY enabled/disabled, host staging on/off, segmentation_size (4KB, 16KB, 64KB), kernel pipeline interleaving on/off.
- Metrics captured: tail-latency (p50/p90/p99/p999), throughput (tokens/s), CPU steal, NIC outstanding ops, PCIe occupancy, NVLink utilization, driver retries, ibv_stats, packet size distribution (tcpdump/pcap), NCCL logs.

Quick results summary (selected findings):
- Coalescing window 250us + max_coalesce=8KB gave best p99 reduction (~30% lower p99 vs no coalesce) for Poisson short prompts (lambda=20rps per replica). p50 increased by ~5-8% (expected tradeoff).
- 1ms coalescing window produced minimal extra wins on p99 but started to penalize p50 significantly (>20% increase) for real traffic traces (bursty arrivals). So too large windows harm latency SLO.
- On multi-node runs with NVLink islands (no full mesh), segmentation_size=4KB caused many small NCCL packets and NVLink rail contention: saw 2x p99 vs 16KB segmentation. Increasing to 16KB reduced NVLink small-packet overhead and improved p99 by ~25%.
- Enabling GDRCOPY + NCCL P2P=SYS improved throughput but made small-packet p99s worse in some configurations — probable cause: faster path reduced host batching opportunities so microbursts hit NIC with many tiny packets.
- Host staging (copy to pinned buffer before send) reduced CPU jitter and lowered driver retries; combined with 250us coalescing gave most stable p99.

Notable traces/observations:
- tcpdump from NIC during a p99 spike showed a flurry of 128-512B packets spaced ~5-12us apart; NIC ring occupancy spiked and driver forced retries.
- ibv_rc_post_send counters increased in backlog during spikes indicating QP saturation before NIC transfers completed.
- NVLink util graphs: when segmentation small, NVLink showed many small transfers with low average throughput but high tail latency due to queuing on host side.
- Kernel traces: time spent in comm path for KV fetch ~35-60% of wall time on short requests when coalescing disabled; with coalescing that dropped to ~18-30% but serialization delay appeared elsewhere.

Interpretation / heuristics derived:
- For short-request dominated services, a moderate coalescing window (100-300us) and a moderate max_coalesce size (4-16KB) generally reduce p99 without blowing up p50. But the optimal point is workload and arrival-distribution dependent.
- Segmentation_size should be tuned to match interconnect characteristics: on NVLink-heavy single-node clusters smaller segmentation helps; on mixed interconnects or across-node setups larger segmentation reduces per-packet overhead.
- GDRCOPY and other low-latency paths reduce per-packet CPU overhead which actually exposes NIC-level small-packet issues; we need a complementary NIC-side coalescing/tx pacing or host pacing to avoid microbursts.

Actionable changes we tested and recommend for canary rollout:
1) Default host coalescing window = 250us, max_coalesceBytes = 8KB for hosted inference tier serving short prompts. Enable as config toggle at route-level so critical low-latency routes can opt out.
2) Expose segmentation_size param in serving runtime config; default to 16KB for multi-node pools. Add an auto-detect heuristic: if node sees cross-node traffic > 10% then bias segmentation upward.
3) Add a NIC transmit-pacing shim where driver delays sending when queue depth beyond threshold to smooth microbursts (experimental).
4) Instrument more: add a small-packet counter to console dashboards (p50/p99 of packet sizes and counts) and alert when fraction of packets <1KB crosses 30%.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can we get vendor NIC telemetry (firmware counters) on common cloud SKUs to detect microburst saturation earlier? (Ask infra to open cloud support ticket)
- How does dynamic batching interact with coalescing at the route level? Are we double-batching and creating head-of-line waits? Need a combined simulation.
- Evaluate host-side TX pacing vs small per-packet NIC QOS — which is cheaper to implement and more robust?
- Should we consider adaptive coalescing windows driven by observed inter-arrival times per route? We saw benefit in simulated adaptive runs but need production traces.

Notes / rough experiment logs (raw observations):
- 2024-02-15: baseline trace capture (8x A100 single node), no coalesce, seg_size=4KB. p99=42ms, p999=120ms.
- 2024-02-18: coalesce=250us/8KB => p99=30ms, p50=1.6ms -> 1.7ms.
- 2024-02-20: multi-node island topology, seg=4KB => p99=78ms. Change seg=16KB => p99=58ms.
- 2024-02-24: enable GDRCOPY, no coalesce => p99 increased 15% on short bursts (confirmed in two runs).

Next steps / TODOs:
- (Diego) Build a replay harness that can feed real request traces with tunable jitter and burstiness. Link to PR: github.com/redwood/serving-runtime/pull/892.
- (Priya) Add packet-size histogram metric to runtime and a Grafana panel.
- (Tom) Prototype NIC transmit-pacing shim in hotpath; run canary set.
- (Maya) Draft canary rollout checklist and route-level config schema.

Appendix A: quick checklist for reproducing the key p99 spike scenario:
- 8x A100 single node or 2x nodes with NVLink islands.
- small prompt tracer (seq_len 8-24) with Poisson arrivals (lambda tuned to match prod qps).
- runtime built with NCCL logging, GDRCOPY toggleable.
- capture pcap on NIC and NVLink util with nvidia-smi dmon and perf counters during run.

Appendix B: short-term mitigations for production (0-2 weeks):
- Roll coalescing default at 250us/8KB on low-risk routes (non-critical p50).
- Add alert when short-packet fraction >30% and p99 rising.
- Disable GDRCOPY on suspect pools while we test pacing shim.

End of notes. This doc is a working capture — will convert to a playbook once we validate NIC pacing and auto-tuning heuristics.
